title: The protective mechanism of taurine deoxycholic acid (TCDCA) through LPAR1 regulation in Buga syndrome

sections.abstract:
The etiology of Budd-Chiari syndrome (BCS), an uncommon but clinically significant condition, remains unclear. Therefore, this study investigates how taurodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA) influences human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs) in BCS. Following TCDCA treatment, the proliferation, apoptosis, migration, inflammatory response, and angiogenesis of HUVECs were examined, along with the levels of cAMP. Transcriptomic sequencing was further performed. Silencing LPAR1 in HUVECs was performed to explore its functional role. The results revealed significantly higher LPAR1 levels in HUVECs compared to controls. Silencing LPAR1 inhibited cell proliferation, migration, inflammation, and angiogenesis, while promoting apoptosis and increasing cAMP levels. Clinical samples from BCS patients showed significant upregulation of LPAR1, supporting our in vitro findings. Our findings suggest that TCDCA plays a pivotal role in BCS by regulating LPAR1.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s40001-025-02945-1.

Keywords: Budd-Chiari syndrome, TCDCA, LPAR1, HUVECs, Angiogenesis
sections.introduction:
BCS can lead to a spectrum of hepatic complications including cirrhosis, ascites, and portal hypertension [ 1 , 2 ]. This syndrome poses a substantial threat to patient survival, with untreated mortality rates reaching 70% within one year and 90% within three years [ 3 ]. Notably, the prevalence and etiological patterns of BCS exhibit marked geographic variations, being more prevalent in Eastern countries like China compared to Western nations [ 4 , 5 ]. Moreover, despite advancements in diagnostic techniques, the incidence of misdiagnosis remains high, often resulting in delayed treatment and poor outcomes. The etiology of BCS is unclear, and although VEC injury is crucial, its mechanism remains elusive. The impact of bile acid TCDCA on VEC and its association with LPAR1 are unknown. This study explores the mechanism by which TCDCA regulates VEC function via LPAR1 to fill the gap and provide a basis for BCS treatment.

Bile acids, particularly taurodeoxycholic acid (TCDCA), have been recognized as crucial components that modulate diverse bodily functions and disease states, including inflammatory responses and cellular functions [ 6 – 8 ]. Moreover, TCDCA influences the caspase-dependent apoptotic pathway in peripheral blood lymphocytes, inhibiting early apoptosis by reducing phosphatidylserine externalization and mitochondrial membrane potential changes at both low and high concentrations [ 9 ]. In immune suppression, TCDCA augments inflammatory responses via immune cell activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine secretion [ 10 ]. Additionally, TCDCA protects HUVECs from damage and stimulates their proliferation and migration [ 11 ].

LPAR1 modulates cell migration, proliferation, and inflammatory responses [ 12 , 13 ]. Previous research has indicated the involvement of LPAR1 in downregulation of cAMP level and cardiovascular pathologies, including platelet activation, endothelial cell adhesion, and neovascularization [ 14 , 15 ]. Given the complex interplay between bile acid metabolism, vascular endothelial cell (VEC) function, and the pathogenesis of BCS, we hypothesize that TCDCA may modulate the pathogenesis of BCS through LPAR1-mediated mechanisms [ 16 – 18 ].

To investigate this hypothesis, we aim to elucidate how TCDCA influences HUVECs in BCS. Furthermore, we aim to identify the role of LPAR1 in mediating these effects, providing insights into novel therapeutic strategies targeting bile acid metabolism and LPAR1 signaling.
sections.discussion:
The etiology of BCS is intricate, encompassing genetic predispositions, hypercoagulable states, and VEC dysfunction. Emerging evidence suggests that the progression of BCS is not solely reliant on hypercoagulability but is also intimately tied to VEC damage. Dang et al. demonstrated that external factors, such as an increased angle of hepatic vein opening and cardiac contraction, could induce persistent VEC damage, triggering an inflammatory response, repair processes, endothelial hyperplasia, and thrombosis, ultimately leading to septal formation and vascular occlusion [ 19 , 20 ]. VECs play a pivotal role in maintaining vascular permeability, regulating angiogenesis, and controlling thrombosis. VEC injury may constitute a core mechanism driving the pathological progression of BCS. Damaged VECs not only release profuse pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic factors but also exacerbate vascular lining damage, creating a vicious cycle.

Moreover, abnormal angiogenesis is a non-negligible factor in the pathogenesis of BCS. Under physiological conditions, angiogenesis occurs through VEC proliferation, migration, and the formation of a neovascular network. However, in BCS, the proliferation of VECs and fibroblasts triggered by venous obstruction, along with VEC migration into the lumen, exacerbates local vascular obstruction and septal-like tissue formation [ 7 ]. Zhang et al. found that the level of long non-coding RNA MTUS2-5 was markedly elevated in extracellular vesicles from BCS patients, and treating cells with these extracellular vesicles enhanced cell proliferation, migration, and angiogenesis, underscoring the importance of angiogenesis in BCS progression [ 21 ]. However, VEC injury caused by venous obstruction in BCS may lead to over-activation of angiogenesis, resulting in abnormal neovascular structures, aggravated local vascular obstruction, and worsening liver damage. In Fig. 1 , the cell viability of the 100 μM TCDCA group at 48 h was higher than that of the 10 μM group. However, the angiogenesis in Fig. 5 did not increase synchronously. This may be because the high concentration induced cell cycle arrest. Although it maintained cell viability, it inhibited angiogenesis-related phenotypes. Further verification of its effect on the cell cycle is needed.

TCDCA, a bile acid, has gradually gained recognition for its multifaceted biological roles in recent years. TCDCA has been implicated in various functions, including alleviating endoplasmic reticulum stress, protecting mitochondria, combating oxidative stress, and even modulating epigenetic processes [ 22 , 23 ]. TCDCA binds to the bile acid receptor, activating the cAMP-PKA-CREB signaling pathway, thereby exerting significant anti-inflammatory effects. Additionally, it modulates the activity of immune cells to mitigate systemic inflammatory responses. Furthermore, TCDCA exerts cytoprotective effects by regulating mitochondrial function and inhibiting endogenous apoptotic pathways. For instance, Cecília et al. demonstrated that TCDCA inhibits apoptosis in the mitochondrial pathway by reducing reactive oxygen species generation, blocking BAX protein activity and cytochrome c release, and maintaining mitochondrial membrane integrity [ 24 ]. Similarly, Yeo et al. found that treating chronic kidney disease-derived hMSCs with TCDCA enhanced mitochondrial function and reduced apoptosis by modulating the PINK1-PrPC-dependent pathway [ 25 ]. Although there is no comparison between the separate siLPAR1 group and the blank group, the difference between the siLPAR1 + TCDCA group and the TCDCA group can indirectly reflect the changing trend of the TCDCA effect after LPAR1 is knocked out. Combining the correlation analysis of the existing data of each group, the impact of LPAR1 knockout on the effect of TCDCA can be deduced, which can tentatively support the rationality of the core conclusion. There are primary and secondary types of BCS patients, and they are often accompanied by complications such as liver cirrhosis and ascites. These differences in clinical classification may affect the expression of LPAR1. Analyzing the expression differences of LPAR1 under different classifications can make the conclusions more in line with clinical practice and enhance the guiding significance for the individualized diagnosis and treatment of BCS. If the expression of LPAR1 in BCS patients is related to a decrease in 1-year survival rate and vascular recanalization rate, it indicates that it can be used as a prognostic indicator, providing a basis for disease risk stratification and targeted therapy, and enhancing the clinical translation significance of the research.

In our study, we investigated how TCDCA impacts on HUVECs in BCS. By assessing angiogenesis and apoptosis-related indices in TCDCA-treated HUVECs, we discovered that TCDCA was involved in modulating HUVEC function. LPA, a bioactive phospholipid, exerts its effects on cells by binding to a series of G-protein-coupled receptors, playing a vital role in regulating VEC migration, proliferation, and differentiation, all essential for angiogenesis [ 26 – 28 ]. Hyperactivation of LPAR1 is also strongly associated with the progression of several fibrotic diseases, especially pulmonary fibrosis, where it promotes collagen deposition by regulating fibroblast proliferation and migration, exacerbating the fibrotic process [ 29 , 30 ]. LPAR1 can participate in lipid metabolism by mediating lipid droplet formation through LPA. Its abnormality may disrupt the lipid homeostasis of VEC and exacerbate damage. Combining with the “lipid-vascular homeostasis” theory can deepen the interpretation of the mechanism by which TCDCA maintains the function of VEC through regulating LPAR1. The in vitro experiment of this study did not simulate in vivo hemodynamics, and the lack of BCS animal model validation may lead to a transformation gap from cellular results to clinical application. Follow-up studies need to be combined with in vivo models to improve the mechanism.

Our experiments further validated these findings, demonstrating that the angiogenic, migration stimulatory, and anti-apoptotic effects of TCDCA were significantly attenuated after LPAR1 knockdown, suggesting that LPAR1 serves as a crucial downstream target for TCDCA to exert its physiological effects. This was evidenced by a significant reduction in Caspase3 and Caspase8 expression in TCDCA-treated cells, along with enhanced angiogenesis and cell migration abilities. Transcriptome sequencing also identified LPAR1 as a significantly upregulated gene under TCDCA treatment, and further experiments confirmed the essential role of LPAR1 activation in the anti-inflammatory effects in the TCDCA-treated cells. However, silencing LPAR1 markedly reversed the effects in the TCDCA-treated cells. The therapeutic potential of TCDCA targeting LPAR1 needs to be analyzed in combination with the impact of anticoagulants such as warfarin on VEC function. If used in combination, it can synergistically improve vascular homeostasis, providing new ideas for the combined treatment of BCS and enhancing its clinical application value.
sections.conclusion: Our findings suggest that TCDCA plays a pivotal role in BCS by regulating LPAR1 signaling pathway. These findings offer a novel insight into future targeted therapies against LPAR1 and is expected to open new avenues for the treatment of BCS and related disorders.
